title: The Wild West of AI: A Legal Tech Reckoning with Ken Crutchfield
author: Ken Crutchfield

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source’s view that current legal AI consists mainly of incremental point solutions is consistent with the cluster’s caution against claiming a settled professional transformation. However, it does not address the cluster’s core proposition about weakened apprenticeship, leverage or partner-succession routes, so its position on that proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Crutchfield accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI currently delivers selective, incremental automation rather than general competence, and that value depends on institutional adoption rather than procurement alone. He materially extends the proposition with concrete implementation priorities: durable data and permissions work, fewer but deeper pilots, sustained vendor support, integration and short-horizon scenario planning.

kp.k: Industrial history frames AI infrastructure and regulatory uncertainty
kp.d: Crutchfield uses railroads, oil and steel as historical analogies for speculative infrastructure investment, scale, cross-industry competition and eventual rule-setting. He interprets US policy as supporting AI leadership and large data centers, while noting that chip-supply strategy spans administrations. These are interpretive parallels, not empirical evidence that AI will follow the same trajectory.
qs: the railroads were the first, if you build it, they will come kind of investment where investors were throwing money to build railroads, literally cities that didn’t exist.
there are some patterns and some things that have happened in the past that if we’re thoughtful about them, it’ll help us inform decisions that we make, how we interpret what’s going on.
We’re operating at massive scale again, and the United States policies are driven towards making sure that the United States leads in AI.

kp.k: Platform advances can strand legal technology investments
kp.d: Crutchfield reports that companies fine-tuning GPT-35 were leapfrogged by 4.0, using this to recommend scenario planning for firms and startups. Shared conversational threads and differentiated medical, legal or therapeutic personas are hypothetical platform developments, not announced capabilities or established confidentiality protections. His proposed planning horizon is the next 18 months to two years.
qs: So many companies, built fine tuning of  of models on GPT-35 and ended up having 4.0 leapfrog that.
Would it make sense for me as a technologist to try to build that? and recognize that wake up one day and it’s all changed because it’s embedded in the scalable systems.
I’m actually gonna try to write an article in the next month or so highlighting a few things that I think might be realistic in the next 18 months to two years.

kp.k: Content disputes may shift toward contracts and restricted access
kp.d: Crutchfield compares AI deployment with Uber entering markets before obtaining permission, predicting lawsuits and likely out-of-court resolutions concerning copyright and data use. For legal information vendors, he anticipates stronger licensing restrictions and less material made available for indexing. Lambert separately characterizes an Anthropic ruling as permitting copied inputs because outputs differ; that is the host's characterization rather than a legal finding established by this transcript.
qs: I think you’re going to see more lawsuits and things that will probably get settled out of court around copyright and theft of data or fair use or whatever it’s going to be interpreted as.
I think now after this, you’re going to see contract law play out a lot more and licensing terms and conditions for access to information.
you might see things no longer be published to be indexed or discoverable and things like that.

kp.k: Editorial enrichment may protect incumbent legal information vendors
kp.d: Crutchfield recalls Thomson Reuters reporting 250 editors improving citation resources before the current generative-AI wave. His hypothetical 90% reduction would still leave 25 people working for several years. He argues that structured citations, page references, legislation and historically correct law complicate substitution by publicly available case law, while asking whether a good-enough competitor could emerge in two years or incumbents remain protected for a decade or longer.
qs: they had 250 editors writing and helping improve and find parallel citations
if the work goes away, that’s still 25 people working for several years full-time
Is the issue in 2012? Okay, what did the law look like in 2012? Those are all things that lawyers need to know.
is there a good enough solution that’s gonna be out there in two years?

kp.k: Large-firm procurement and integration impose substantial vendor hurdles
kp.d: Crutchfield says startups underestimate large firms' customization expectations, perfection standards, SOC 2 audits and corporate-client policy requirements. He recommends considering mid-market firms or corporate legal buyers. Fragmented legal workflows favor specialist products, but integrating them is necessary for a comprehensive client view and cross-selling; practice-specific silos may work locally while sacrificing that wider view.
qs: their standard is perfection, even if good enough could be good enough.
consider mid-market firms if you’re looking at law firms or is there a corporate legal angle that you can go after
the standards that are being required for, you know, SOC 2 audits and conforming with policies of corporate clients are pretty significant.
It’s possible that a practice area might be able to adopt something within the practice area that’s relatively siloed. And that might be just fine, except you lose that 360 view the client.

kp.k: Repeatable transformative applications remain elusive in his experience
kp.d: Crutchfield characterizes much current legal AI as incremental automation rather than a widely repeatable must-have application comparable to early online legal research. He identifies squeezing out 20 to 30 % of non-billable time and automating parts of SEC filings as useful possibilities, not measured results. His skepticism also encompasses Harvey: he says he has not heard sufficiently specific, repeatable use cases, while qualifying his assessment of large firms' custom deployments as an outside-in perception.
qs: Getting rid of the 20 to 30 % of non-billable time that can be squeezed out without affecting the billable hour, that’s great.
but I’m really not even hearing, even like with Harvey and others, what are the specific things that are repeatable that everybody’s saying, I gotta have that?
I think there’s a lot of incrementalism and a lot of things that show promise long-term to do that.
And some of the really large firms that are doing things that are custom with Harvey, that’s my outside in perception.  that’s not repeatable yet.

kp.k: AI branding yields to integrated workflow expectations
kp.d: From his observations of AALL exhibition booths, Crutchfield suggests AI is becoming an expected product component rather than the headline differentiator. Responding to Lambert's concern about buying numerous narrow products to assemble one useful package, he argues for stitching solutions together into more complete workflows. This is a qualitative market observation, not a systematic vendor survey.
qs: AI was not the headline.
it’s kind of fading into being like an expected component of what’s there.
there’s going to have to be a little bit more stitching together, integrating, pulling together things to do more complete workflows.

kp.k: Data acquisition scenarios coexist with continued market fragmentation
kp.d: Asked by Lambert about Microsoft buying Thomson Reuters, Crutchfield treats vertical-data acquisitions as plausible scenario-planning possibilities, expressly disclaiming inside knowledge. He nevertheless expects established legal vendors to retain strong positions and the number of providers to grow before shrinking, because so many fragmented tasks remain available for automation. He does not endorse the host's suggestion that legal information will soon consolidate into a few politically differentiated blocs.
qs: I have no knowledge, but it just seems like intuitively that  there would be somebody thinking and asking those questions
are there data sources in particular industries or areas that have, pervasive, important, deep vertical like medical or other things
I think they’ve got really strong positions, and I think they’re going to continue to have strong positions.
I think you’re gonna see a lot more companies before you see a lot less.

kp.k: Data hygiene is a durable investment across model changes
kp.d: Crutchfield's strongest operational recommendation is to improve data, metadata and access permissions, because that work remains useful when models or vendors change. He argues that fragmented knowledge management and lawyers' private document stores must be addressed. He also reports firms' concerns that email contains speculation, jokes and hypotheticals, making categorization important when AI must produce substantively correct answers.
qs: If there’s one thing that’s going to be work that’s valuable that will survive a change in language models
Get your data right. Get the metadata straight. Figure out your permissions and who can have access and get access to that.

If your knowledge management systems are fragmented because you still have some rogue attorneys that like to keep things on a flash drive or coddled away somewhere, those things have got to break down.
there’s a lot of speculation in email, not all email is official documents.

kp.k: Hourly billing complicates demonstrating AI investment returns
kp.d: Crutchfield argues that hourly-billing infrastructure perpetuates existing incentives and that firms typically lack metrics for margin improvement on fixed-fee matters. Lambert separately says he does not know a firm able to claim a huge return on its AI investment; this is a host observation, not measured industry evidence. When Gebauer asks about return on experience, Crutchfield instead frames learning and using evolving tools as a prospective cost of doing business.
qs: Their infrastructure is structured to perpetuate that.
they don’t have metrics on improving margin and fixed fee engagements and things like that typically.
I find that ROI is always going to be a bit of a challenge.  with the billable hour in firms.
I kind of rephrase it and say it’s the new cost of doing business.

kp.k: Client demands could make AI capability competitively necessary
kp.d: Crutchfield recounts a firm's report that it secured an engagement because the client required machine learning and competing firms lacked that capability. He predicts clients may rapidly move from prohibiting AI to requiring it, forcing fast followers to catch up with technology leaders. His reference to future professional misconduct is part of that speculative reversal, not a statement of an existing professional rule.
qs: Their client said, I want you to do this engagement using machine learning.
when the other vendors or when the other firms were asked, they did not have a machine learning capability.

I think that switch flips like that.

kp.k: Vendors should prioritize depth over broad feature coverage
kp.d: Against rapid agent developments, Crutchfield recommends stepping back, focusing on a specific problem and deepening the solution through successive releases rather than attempting everything. He asserts that ChatGPT can log into Thomson or Lexis accounts and perform tasks on users' behalf, but provides no demonstration or performance evidence. Bloomberg's willingness to continue beyond an initial release supplies his organizational example of sustained product development.
qs: now ChatGPT can log into your Thomson account or your Lexis account and do certain things on your behalf.
Don’t, don’t try to cover the waterfront and do everything.
solve a specific problem, build out from that, build out again, build out again.
they’d go deeper and they’d dig into a second, a third, and a fourth release.

kp.k: Adoption requires funded change management beyond signing contracts
kp.d: Crutchfield warns vendors that unused products risk cancellation and says successful sales require process redesign, training, skill changes and demonstrated outcomes. Firms must budget for non-billable implementation work despite its perceived impact on partner profits. He recommends strong onboarding and customer success even for apparently low-implementation SaaS, using early Lexis's full-service infrastructure and on-site support as an analogy rather than demanding identical arrangements today.
qs: the sale isn’t over until you have users actually using the product. Otherwise, you have a contract that’s likely to get canceled.
get through the process of changing their process, ⁓ understanding what the skill set changes are in the training and make sure that they’re getting the outcomes that are needed.
I think there needs to be strong onboarding customer success sorts of approaches.
there’s probably a cost and a charge for some of that work to truly get to adoption with some of these solutions.

kp.k: Leadership sponsorship and meaningful metrics should guide project selection
kp.d: Crutchfield recommends defining success before purchasing or starting a project, securing leadership commitment and recognizing sponsors' political, reputational and personal stakes. He advocates fewer pilots pursued further, with durable data work alongside them. Where direct operational metrics are weak, client requests and comparator firms' capabilities can become signals that competitive parity justifies adoption; otherwise a project may not yet warrant proceeding.
qs: focusing a little bit more on fewer tasks, fewer pilots, and trying to get a few more of them, really kind of progress them further.
think about those things before you decide to pursue a project or to buy what would success look like?
In a firm make sure you’ve got some leadership skin in the game on it.
if those metrics don’t matter, then maybe it’s not time to do the work or to do the project
the metric is competitive parity.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Crutchfield anticipates incremental workflow automation, competitive pressure to adopt AI, and continuing disruption of legal-tech products by general-purpose platforms, rather than an already-established universal legal AI killer application.
pts.d: Ken Crutchfield argues that many current legal AI offerings are incremental point solutions and that more integration is needed to deliver complete workflows; he describes bespoke work with Harvey at large firms as not yet repeatable, explicitly qualifying this as an outside-in perception. He sees opportunities to reduce non-billable work without undermining hourly billing, but does not report measured savings. He warns that advances in foundation models can leapfrog developers' investments and speculates that general-purpose platforms could incorporate collaboration or professional personas now contemplated by specialist developers. For legal information publishers, he predicts greater reliance on contracts, licensing and restrictions on indexing to protect content. He treats the adequacy of open case-law alternatives and the durability of proprietary editorial assets as unresolved competitive questions. Acquisition of a legal information company by a major technology platform is a scenario, not a reported transaction. Despite strong incumbent positions, he expects more legal-tech companies before eventual contraction because substantial automation opportunities remain. He argues that data hygiene, metadata and access permissions are durable investments across model changes, while poorly classified email can contaminate substantive answers. He predicts that client demands could rapidly turn AI capability into a competitive requirement, and that proficiency will increasingly be necessary for legal practice. Separately, introductory guest Nikki Shaver claims that newer providers, including Smart-esque and AI-native law firm Covenant, are automating fund-practice processes that were difficult to automate before generative AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is principally professional experience, informal observations, unnamed-firm anecdotes and historical analogy; the transcript supplies no systematic legal AI performance or ROI study.
pts.d: Crutchfield draws on his work at legal information vendors, including early Lexis adoption and Bloomberg's sustained product development. His observation that AI is becoming an expected product component comes from reviewing vendor booths at AALL. His skepticism about repeatable transformative applications is expressly framed as what he is hearing and seeing, not a benchmark result. He cites developers' GPT-3.5 fine-tuning being leapfrogged by a later model as an example of investment obsolescence, without identifying companies or quantifying losses. He recalls Thomson Reuters reporting 250 editors working on citation-related improvements, then uses a hypothetical 90% reduction to illustrate residual work; these are not demonstrated AI productivity findings. For competitive demand, he recounts an unnamed firm obtaining work because a client required machine learning and competing firms lacked it. For data risks, he reports unnamed firms' concerns about speculative email and refers to advice from a contact formerly involved in Google's self-driving initiative. His adoption recommendations draw on historical Lexis installation and embedded support practices. Railroad and industrial-development analogies underpin platform-scale and consolidation scenarios. He explicitly disclaims inside knowledge of a possible major-platform acquisition. Shaver identifies market entrants and manual fund workflows but provides no measured error reduction, time savings or profitability results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Crutchfield describes an early, rapidly changing market, with conditional scenarios rather than firm deadlines for transformation.
pts.d: In this 2025 discussion, Crutchfield regards legal AI as still in its early days. He proposes developing scenarios for what major model providers might deliver over the next 18 months to two years; this is a planned scenario exercise, not a claim that particular features will arrive on that schedule. He contrasts a possible good-enough legal information competitor in two years with a proprietary publisher's possible protection for a decade or longer, leaving both as questions. He expects expansion before contraction but gives no date for consolidation. Client-led adoption pressure is conditional on clients shifting from restricting AI to requiring it; his reference to possible professional misconduct is part of that anticipated shift, not a statement that current rules universally require AI. Realizing benefits depends on usable and appropriately permissioned data, workflow integration, user adoption, training, sponsorship and agreed measures of success. Hourly billing structures complicate conventional ROI assessments, making competitive parity a possible alternative rationale. He recommends fewer, more developed pilots and warns that a platform release could fundamentally change current projects. His forecasts of improving tools and required proficiency extend broadly through the twenty-first century without a precise endpoint.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary affected groups are law firms, their clients and implementation teams, legal-tech startups, and incumbent legal information publishers.
pts.d: For large firms, Crutchfield identifies demanding customization, security and corporate-client compliance requirements as barriers to buying and deploying products. Practice-area solutions can enable local adoption while sacrificing a complete view of the client. He suggests that startups consider mid-market firms or corporate legal departments as alternative customer segments, rather than treating all firms as interchangeable buyers. Legal-tech vendors face both model-driven product obsolescence and cancellation risk if contracts fail to produce actual use; they may need deeper onboarding, customer success and implementation support. Incumbent publishers face challenges to their content protection and competitive differentiation, while retaining strong positions and potentially valuable editorial infrastructure. Lawyers must develop tool proficiency and share appropriately governed knowledge rather than retain inaccessible personal stores. Partners and firm leaders must accept training and change-management costs that do not immediately generate billable time. Internal sponsors expend political capital and put personal reputations at stake. Corporate clients can influence which firms win work through technology requirements. Shaver's fund-practice example concerns large firms, associates performing manual copying, and providers automating side-letter negotiation and most-favored-nation elections. The discussion does not offer a concrete prediction of lawyer headcount reductions, staffing-shape changes or expanded access to justice.
